notes: UNOFFICIAL SOURCE: the official CISCE document could not be opened (cisce.org was unreachable from the build environment). The themes and outcomes come from a third-party copy of the Class V mathematics pages, read through a text summary, so every theme is verified:false.

CISCE is understood not to prescribe a textbook for Class V (not checked against an official statement): each school chooses its own books and may order or extend the topics differently. Check this inventory against the school's actual textbook and term plan.

The document lists 78 learning-outcome lines in ten themes. They are written here as 75 outcomes in OpenPath's own words (lines that repeat a skill are merged, and the line on pie charts and line graphs is split in two), plus 2 items that appear only under key concepts (tables to 20; dividing fractions): 77 in all. 70 are mapped (56 fully, 14 partly: see each outcome's coverage and note). 7 are not in the release and are listed under gaps: 3 have no OpenPath skill, and 4 (number line, and the meaning, comparing and ordering of integers) have questions but a lesson that fails OpenPath's teaching checks.
A chapter here is a theme of the curriculum, in the document's order; the curriculum has no sections.
No competency is proposed by this file: every outcome is mapped to competencies that already exist, and reuses the CBSE and Tamil Nadu Grade 5 mappings where the outcome is the same.

Several mapped competencies were written for Grade 6 or 7 in the other boards (integers, multiplying and dividing fractions and decimals, prime factorisation, divisibility, Indian and international numeration, percentage of an amount). CISCE places them in Class V; their lessons and questions were written with older learners in mind.

outcomes.statement: Read and write numbers up to crores with Indian place value and commas.
Read and write large numbers in the international system (millions) and relate it to lakhs and crores.
Write a large number in expanded form and turn an expanded form back into the number.
Compare large numbers by place value and put them in ascending or descending order.
Make the greatest and the smallest number from a set of digits.
Round a number to the nearest 10, 100 or 1000.
Show what a fraction means as equal parts of a whole.
Find a fraction of a collection of objects.
Recognise and make equivalent fractions.
Write simple fractions such as a half, a quarter and a fifth as decimals and back, with lengths and money.
Build and use the multiplication tables from 2 to 20.
outcomes.source: Theme 1, key concept (no outcome line of its own) (p. 101 onwards)
outcomes.note: Facts to 10 × 10 and the 13 to 19 tables have questions; 11, 12 and 20 have none of their own.

outcomes.statement: Write numbers in Roman numerals.

proposed.name: Read and write Roman numerals
proposed.why: No existing competency covers Roman numerals; reading one adds and takes away the values of its place parts.

outcomes.statement: Use place value beyond 1000 when adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing.
Divide a number by a two-digit number with the standard written method.
outcomes.source: Theme 2, learning outcomes 2 and 5 (the same skill, listed twice) (p. 103 onwards)

outcomes.statement: Estimate a sum, difference, product or quotient, and check an answer against the estimate.
outcomes.note: Estimating a quotient of whole numbers has no question of its own.

outcomes.statement: Add, subtract and multiply large numbers with the standard written methods.
Solve everyday problems that need the four operations.
Make up a word problem that fits a given number statement.
outcomes.note: OpenPath asks which operation fits a story; a problem the learner writes needs a person to read it.

outcomes.statement: Explain what factors, multiples, prime numbers and composite numbers are.
Find factors and multiples in different ways, including a factor tree.
Pick out the prime and the composite numbers up to 100.
Tell proper fractions, improper fractions and mixed numbers apart.
Write equivalent fractions by multiplying or dividing the top and bottom numbers by the same number.
Compare and order three or more fractions.
Add and subtract unlike fractions and mixed numbers.
Solve word problems that add or subtract fractions.
outcomes.note: The questions on adding and subtracting fractions are calculations, not stories.

outcomes.statement: Read a fraction 'of' a quantity as a multiplication.
Multiply a fraction by a whole number and a fraction by a fraction.
Divide a whole number by a fraction and a fraction by a fraction.
outcomes.source: Theme 3, key concept (no outcome line of its own) (p. 105 onwards)

outcomes.statement: Write fractions with denominator 10, 100 or 1000 as decimals and back.
Show a decimal in a picture, such as a shaded strip or grid.
outcomes.note: Decimals are asked in figures and words; shaded-grid pictures of decimals are not part of the questions.

outcomes.statement: Give the place value of each digit of a decimal to thousandths.
Write a decimal in expanded form.
Recognise equivalent decimals, like decimals and unlike decimals.
outcomes.note: Decimals with different numbers of places are compared; the names 'like' and 'unlike' decimals are not used.

outcomes.statement: Compare decimals and put them in order.
outcomes.source: Theme 3, learning outcomes 13 (compare and order) (p. 105 onwards)

outcomes.statement: Add and subtract decimals.
Solve word problems that add or subtract decimals.
Multiply a decimal by 10, 100 or 1000 by moving the digits.
Multiply a decimal by a whole number and a decimal by a decimal.

chapters.title: Theme 4: Playing with Numbers (Factors and Multiples)

outcomes.statement: List the multiples of a number.
Find all the factors of a number.
Identify prime, composite, twin-prime and co-prime numbers.
outcomes.note: Prime, composite and co-prime numbers have questions; twin primes have none.

outcomes.statement: Test whether a number is divisible by 2, 3, 4, 5, 9, 10 or 11.
outcomes.source: Theme 4, learning outcome 4 and its key concept (p. 107 onwards)
outcomes.note: The questions cover the tests for 2, 4, 5, 8 and 10 and a missing-digit question; 3, 9 and 11 are not practised as tests of their own.

outcomes.statement: Write a number as a product of its prime factors with a factor tree.
Find the HCF of numbers by listing factors and by common division.
Find the LCM of numbers by listing multiples and by common division.
Use the link HCF × LCM = product of the two numbers to find one from the other.
Add and subtract integers.
Place whole numbers on a number line.
Understand integers as the counting numbers, zero and the negatives of the counting numbers.
outcomes.note: The lesson explains negative numbers on a number line and the questions order integers; no question asks what an integer is.

outcomes.statement: Compare two integers using a number line.
Put integers in ascending or descending order.
outcomes.note: Questions ask for increasing order (smallest first); none asks for descending order.

outcomes.statement: Find angles in shapes and in the surroundings, by looking and by folding paper.
outcomes.note: Paper folding is a hands-on activity outside OpenPath.

outcomes.statement: Spot right angles in objects and pictures.
Classify an angle as right, acute or obtuse.
outcomes.source: Theme 6, learning outcomes 2 and 6 (the same skill, listed twice) (p. 110 onwards)

outcomes.statement: Draw and trace acute, obtuse and right angles, and read the size of an angle.
outcomes.source: Theme 6, learning outcome 7 and the key concept on angle measures (p. 110 onwards)
outcomes.note: Reading an angle from a protractor is practised; a drawn angle needs a person to check it.

outcomes.statement: Recognise reflection symmetry and rotational symmetry in familiar 2-D shapes and letters.
Make cubes, cuboids, cylinders and cones from their nets.
outcomes.note: Matching solids with nets is practised; folding a real net is a hands-on activity outside OpenPath.

outcomes.statement: Explore symmetry in familiar 3-D shapes.

proposed.name: Find mirror symmetry in familiar 3-D shapes
proposed.why: symmetry-lines and symmetry-fold are about flat shapes; a mirror cut of a solid extends a line of symmetry of its face.

outcomes.statement: Relate larger and smaller units of length, weight, capacity, time and money, and convert both ways.
Estimate how much a solid or a container holds in a known unit, such as mugs in a bucket.
Use the four operations in problems about money, length, mass, capacity and intervals of time.
Say what the area and the perimeter of a simple shape are.
Work out the area and the perimeter of simple shapes such as rectangles and squares.
Understand a percentage as a fraction with denominator 100.
Relate fractions, decimals and percentages to one another.
Show a percentage in a picture, such as a shaded hundred grid.
outcomes.note: Percentages are asked in figures; shaded-grid pictures are not part of the questions.

outcomes.statement: Change a fraction into a percentage and a percentage into a fraction.
Change a decimal into a percentage and a percentage into a decimal.
Solve simple word problems about percentages.
Collect everyday data, record it in a table, show it in a bar graph and read a given bar graph.
outcomes.note: Collecting data and drawing a graph by hand are outside OpenPath.

outcomes.statement: Read a pie chart of the kind printed in newspapers and magazines.
Read a line graph of the kind printed in newspapers and magazines.

proposed.name: Read line graphs of data
proposed.why: bar-charts reads separate bars against a scale; a line graph adds change over time read from the same kind of scale.

outcomes.statement: Find the repeating unit of a pattern and continue the pattern.
Find the rule of a growing pattern and use it to continue the pattern.
Make a pattern that changes in more than one way at once, such as shape and colour.
outcomes.note: Continuing a pattern is practised; a pattern the learner invents needs a person to look at it.

outcomes.statement: See and describe the patterns in triangular numbers and square numbers.
